subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
extraLines: 1. What are the steps involved in the process of psychological assessment?
Assessment begins with a referral, in which a question is posed about a client (for example
by a physician, teacher, court or the client himself). The psychologist then plans the
assessment, gathers information through interviews, observation and psychological tests,
and develops a case history. The data are then interpreted and integrated, a diagnosis or
formulation is made, and finally the findings are communicated in a report with
recommendations for treatment or other decisions, followed where needed by follow-up.
2. What is fraudulent data in research, and why is it an ethical problem?
Fraudulent data means fabricating, falsifying or misrepresenting research data — for
example inventing results that were never collected or altering findings to fit a hypothesis. It
is a serious ethical violation because science depends on honesty and accuracy; fabricated
data mislead other researchers, waste resources, damage the credibility of the profession
and can lead to harmful decisions when the false findings are applied to real clients.
3. Differentiate between description and explanation in clinical psychology.
Description means stating what a behaviour or problem is like — its signs, symptoms,
frequency and course — without saying why it occurs. Explanation goes a step further and
accounts for why the problem occurs, identifying its causes and underlying mechanisms,
usually on the basis of a theory. Description answers the question 'what?', whereas
explanation answers the question 'why?'. Good clinical work needs both: an accurate
description of the problem and a sound explanation that guides treatment.
4. Differentiate between personal history and social history in a case history
interview.
Personal history covers the individual's own life story: birth and early development,
schooling, health and illnesses, habits, marital life and previous psychological problems and
treatment. Social history covers the person's relationships and social context: family
background and relationships, friendships, occupation and work relationships, social
activities and the support system available to the person. Together they give the clinician a
complete picture of the client and the environment in which the problem developed.
5. How are fees and financial arrangements handled in clinical practice?
Fees and financial arrangements should be discussed and agreed upon openly at the very
beginning of the professional relationship, preferably before or at the start of therapy, so
that there is no misunderstanding later. The psychologist should be honest about charges,
billing, missed-session policy and insurance arrangements, keep accurate financial records,
and never exploit the client financially. Barter or unusual arrangements that could harm the
therapeutic relationship or exploit the client should be avoided, and inability to pay should
be handled ethically, for example by referral to a low-cost service.
6. What is a crisis interview? Discuss its features and purpose.
A crisis interview is conducted when the patient is in the middle of a significant, often
traumatic or life-threatening situation, such as a suicide attempt, a disaster or an acute loss.
Its purpose is immediate: to assess the nature and severity of the crisis, evaluate the risk of
harm to self or others, provide emotional support, and plan immediate intervention and
safety measures. It is focused, directive and brief, and it aims to stabilise the person rather
than to explore long-standing personality issues.
7. Name and briefly explain the three types of true experimental design.
(1) The pretest-posttest control group design, in which participants are randomly assigned to
experimental and control groups and measured before and after the treatment. (2) The
posttest-only control group design, in which randomly assigned groups are measured only
after the treatment, avoiding pretest effects. (3) The Solomon four-group design, which
combines the first two designs in four groups to control for the effect of pretesting itself.
Random assignment is the essential feature that makes these 'true' experimental designs.
8. Who is the founder of clinical psychology, and why is he called so?
Lightner Witmer is regarded as the founder of clinical psychology. In 1896 he established the
first psychological clinic at the University of Pennsylvania, where children with learning and
behavioural problems were assessed and treated. In 1907 he founded the first journal of the
field, The Psychological Clinic, and it was Witmer who first used the term 'clinical
psychology'. His clinic became the model for applying psychological science to the
assessment and treatment of individual problems.
9. Write a note on the Simon-Binet intelligence test.
The Simon-Binet test was developed in France by Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon (1905) to
identify school children who needed special help. It presented tasks arranged in order of
increasing difficulty and introduced the concept of mental age — the level of performance
typical of children of a given age. It was later revised at Stanford University by Lewis Terman
as the Stanford-Binet test, which used the intelligence quotient, IQ = (Mental Age /
Chronological Age) x 100. It was the first practical, standardised intelligence test and laid the
foundation of modern intelligence testing.
10. How does clinical psychology differ from other branches of psychology?
Clinical psychology is concerned with the assessment, diagnosis, treatment and prevention
of mental and behavioural disorders in individuals, integrating science and practice. Other
branches have different focuses: counselling psychology deals with relatively mild
adjustment problems of normal people; school psychology works with learning and
behaviour problems in educational settings; industrial/organizational psychology applies
psychology to workplaces; and experimental psychology studies basic processes in
laboratory research. Clinical psychology is distinguished by its focus on psychopathology and
its work with seriously disturbed individuals in clinical settings.
11. Describe any three types of validity.
(1) Content validity: the extent to which a test adequately samples the behaviour or domain
it is meant to measure. (2) Predictive validity: the extent to which test scores accurately
predict some behaviour or event in the future, such as success in a job or course. (3)
Concurrent validity: the extent to which test scores agree with a criterion measured at the
same time, such as another established test of the same trait. (Construct validity — whether
the test truly measures the theoretical construct — is another major type.)
12. What makes an interview effective? Discuss the factors involved in effective
interviewing.
An effective interview depends on good rapport, active listening, empathy, appropriate
questioning, and attention to both verbal and non-verbal behaviour. The interviewer should
create a comfortable, private and non-judgmental atmosphere, ask clear open-ended as well
as focused questions, avoid leading questions and premature interpretation, and summarise
and clarify what the client says. Risks and barriers include the interviewer's biases, the halo
effect, over-interpretation, poor listening and cultural differences, all of which must be
guarded against for the interview to yield valid information.
13. State the points McFall argued in his 1991 'call to action' (manifesto) for
clinical psychology.
Richard McFall's 1991 manifesto argued that: (1) scientific clinical psychology is the only
legitimate and acceptable form of clinical psychology; (2) psychological services should not
be administered to the public unless they have been shown to be effective through scientific
research; and (3) training in clinical psychology must be grounded in rigorous scientific
methods, so applied work that ignores the scientific evidence base is unacceptable. His
central demand was that clinical practice must rest on scientifically demonstrated
effectiveness.
14. What is play therapy? Explain its role in clinical psychology.
Play therapy is a form of psychotherapy for children in which play — toys, games, drawing
and dramatisation — is used as the medium of communication and treatment, because
children express their feelings and conflicts more naturally through play than through words.
It is grounded in psychoanalytic theory and was developed further by workers such as Anna
Freud and Melanie Klein. In clinical psychology it helps the clinician understand the child's
inner world, allows the child to work through anxiety and conflicts, and builds a therapeutic
relationship with the child.
15. What are intelligence tests? Discuss their uses in clinical psychology.
Intelligence tests are standardised psychological tests designed to measure a variety of
mental functions such as reasoning, comprehension, memory and judgment, and to express
them as a score such as IQ. Famous examples include the Stanford-Binet test, the Wechsler
scales (WAIS for adults and WISC for children) and the group tests Army Alpha (verbal) and
Army Beta (nonverbal). Clinically they are used to assess intellectual disability, identify
giftedness, plan education and rehabilitation, and contribute to neuropsychological and
diagnostic evaluation.
16. Define abnormal behaviour. Discuss disability or dysfunction as a criterion of
abnormality.
Abnormal behaviour is behaviour that deviates from social norms, causes subjective
distress, and interferes with a person's functioning. According to the disability or dysfunction
criterion, behaviour is abnormal when it creates some degree of social, interpersonal or
occupational problems for the individual — the person cannot perform expected roles at
home, at work or in society. Critically, this criterion is practical and observable, but it
depends on social expectations and culture: the same behaviour may disable a person in
one setting and not in another, and some disturbed people function outwardly well, so
dysfunction alone cannot define abnormality.
17. Discuss the role of women psychologists during the Second World War.
During the Second World War many male psychologists joined the armed services, and
women psychologists stepped into clinical and counselling roles in hospitals, clinics and
veterans' services. Organisations of women psychologists and counsellors coordinated
training and placement, and women provided assessment and counselling to soldiers and
their families. The war demonstrated women's competence in applied psychology, expanded
their professional opportunities, and after the war many continued in clinical work,
contributing significantly to the growth of clinical and counselling psychology.
18. Discuss the significance and contributions of the 19th century to clinical
psychology.
The 19th century laid the scientific foundations of clinical psychology. Humane treatment of
the mentally ill was promoted by reformers such as Philippe Pinel; Wilhelm Wundt
established the first psychology laboratory in 1879, making psychology an experimental
science; Francis Galton pioneered individual differences and mental measurement; James
McKeen Cattell introduced mental tests; Emil Kraepelin developed the classification of
mental disorders; and Lightner Witmer, at the century's end, founded the first psychological
clinic in 1896. These contributions gave clinical psychology its science, its measurement
tools and its first clinical setting.
19. State the standard ethical principles that guide clinical psychologists.
The standard ethical principles include: beneficence and non-maleficence (doing good and
avoiding harm to clients), fidelity and responsibility (honesty, keeping commitments and
professional responsibility), integrity (truthfulness in practice, teaching and research), justice
(fair and equal access to psychological services), and respect for people's rights and dignity,
which includes confidentiality, privacy and informed consent. In practice these appear as
keeping confidentiality, obtaining informed consent, practising within one's competence,
avoiding exploitation and harm, and providing services in emergencies.
20. Describe the types of variables used in psychological research.
(1) Independent variable: the variable manipulated by the researcher to observe its effect.
(2) Dependent variable: the variable that is measured and is expected to change as a result
of the manipulation. (3) Extraneous or confounding variables: other factors that may
influence the dependent variable and must be controlled. Variables are also classified as
quantitative or qualitative, and as discrete (countable, separate values) or continuous (any
value within a range).
21. Write a note on the survey method of research.
The survey method collects information from a large number of people, usually through
questionnaires or interviews, about their attitudes, opinions, behaviour or characteristics. It
is economical, can cover a large and representative sample, and is useful for studying
variables that cannot be manipulated experimentally. Its limitations include response bias —
respondents may say what they think the researcher wants to hear (demand characteristics)
or answer carelessly — and the fact that it shows associations rather than causes. Careful
sampling, well-designed questions and anonymity improve its quality.
22. Differentiate between degree and direction of a relationship between
variables.
Direction of relationship tells whether the variables move together in the same direction
(positive relationship — both increase or both decrease) or in opposite directions (negative
relationship — one increases as the other decreases). Degree of relationship tells how strong
the association is, expressed by the correlation coefficient, which ranges from -1.00 to
+1.00: values near +1 or -1 show a strong relationship, while values near 0 show a weak or
no relationship.
23. Discuss the benefits of a career in psychology from a clinical psychologist's
point of view.
A career in clinical psychology offers the satisfaction of helping people overcome their
struggles and seeing positive change in their lives, a sense of fulfilment and purpose in
meaningful work, intellectual variety because every client and problem is different,
opportunities for research and teaching, and respectable financial rewards and benefits that
allow a comfortable life. As illustrated by Sara, a clinical psychologist, the combination of
serving others and personal and professional growth makes the career highly rewarding.
24. When was the American Psychological Society established, and why?
The American Psychological Society (APS) was established in 1988. It was founded by
psychologists who felt that the American Psychological Association (APA) was giving more
attention to practitioners than to the science of psychology; the APS was therefore created
to promote, protect and advance the interests of scientifically oriented psychology in
research, application, teaching and public policy. (It should not be confused with the APA
itself, which was founded in 1892.)
25. What is a referral, and why is it important in the assessment process?
A referral is the request or direction through which a client comes to the psychologist — from
a physician, teacher, court, another professional, an agency, or the client himself — usually
accompanied by a specific referral question. It is important because the assessment process
begins with the referral: it defines the problem to be assessed, the decisions the assessment
must inform, and the person or agency to whom the findings must be communicated. A clear
referral question keeps the assessment focused and useful.
26. Write a note on the case history interview.
The case history interview is an interview in which the clinician systematically gathers the
history of the client's problem and life: the presenting complaint and its onset and course,
previous illnesses and treatment, personal history (development, education, health, habits,
marital life) and social history (family, relationships, occupation and social functioning). It
provides the background against which test results and present behaviour are interpreted,
helps in diagnosis and treatment planning, and builds rapport with the client.
27. Briefly describe behaviourism and social learning theory.
Behaviourism, founded by John B. Watson and developed by B. F. Skinner, holds that
psychology should study observable behaviour, and that behaviour is learned through
conditioning — classical conditioning (Pavlov) and operant conditioning (reinforcement and
punishment). Social learning theory, proposed by Albert Bandura (also called social cognitive
theory), adds that people also learn by observing and imitating models, and that cognitive
factors such as expectations and self-efficacy mediate learning. Both approaches strongly
influenced behavioural assessment and therapy in clinical psychology.
28. Discuss the role of women counsellors' associations during the Second World
War.
During the Second World War, associations of women counsellors organised and mobilised
trained women to fill the shortage of counsellors created by men leaving for military service.
They helped in recruiting, training and placing women counsellors in hospitals, military
settings, schools and community agencies, and supported counselling services for soldiers,
veterans and their families. Their work kept mental health services running during the war
and established women as an essential part of the counselling and clinical workforce.
29. What is an intelligence test? Differentiate between individual and group
intelligence tests.
An intelligence test is a standardised test designed to measure mental abilities such as
reasoning, comprehension and judgment and to yield a score such as IQ. Individual tests,
such as the Stanford-Binet and the Wechsler scales, are administered to one person at a
time by a trained examiner; they allow close observation but are time-consuming and costly.
Group tests, such as Army Alpha (verbal) and Army Beta (nonverbal), can be given to many
people at once; they are economical and were developed for mass screening, especially of
army recruits, but give less clinical information about each person.
30. What is the scientist-practitioner (Boulder) model of training in clinical
psychology?
The scientist-practitioner model, adopted at the Boulder Conference of 1949, holds that
clinical psychologists should be trained both as scientists and as practitioners. The PhD
programme therefore combines rigorous training in research methods and the production of
original research (the dissertation) with supervised clinical training through practicum and
internship. Its aim is that practice should be grounded in science and that clinicians should
be able to evaluate and contribute to research throughout their careers.
31. Differentiate between clinical psychology and psychiatry.
Clinical psychology is a branch of psychology: its practitioners hold a master's or doctoral
degree in psychology (MA/MSc, PhD or PsyD), and they specialise in psychological
assessment, diagnosis and psychotherapy, but they do not prescribe medication. Psychiatry
is a branch of medicine: psychiatrists hold a medical degree (MBBS) followed by residency
training in psychiatry, approach mental illness from a medical standpoint, and can prescribe
medication and other physical treatments. The two professions often work together as part
of a mental health team.
32. What is meant by informed consent in clinical research and practice?
Informed consent is the prior permission given by a client or research participant after being
fully informed about the purpose, procedures, possible risks and benefits, and his or her
rights, including the right to refuse or withdraw at any time without penalty. It must be given
voluntarily and by a person competent to decide. Informed consent protects the dignity and
autonomy of clients and participants and is a basic ethical requirement of both clinical
practice and research.
33. Discuss the contributions of the Greeks to the understanding of mental illness.
The Greeks made the first naturalistic attempts to explain mental illness. Hippocrates held
that psychological problems, like physical illnesses, were caused by imbalances in the four
bodily humours and rejected supernatural explanations, linking the brain with thought and
disturbance. Plato viewed mental disturbance in terms of conflict within the soul, and
Aristotle contributed early accounts of emotion and cognition. Greek thought also associated
conditions such as mental retardation with magic and religion in popular belief, but the
Hippocratic naturalistic approach laid the foundation for a medical and scientific view of
mental illness.
34. What is DSM? Discuss its role in the diagnosis of psychological problems.
DSM is the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, published by the American
Psychiatric Association. It provides standard names, definitions and diagnostic criteria for
mental disorders, so that clinicians and researchers use the same language. In the multiaxial
system of DSM-IV, disorders were recorded on five axes — for example clinical disorders on
Axis I, personality disorders on Axis II, general medical conditions on Axis III, and
psychosocial and environmental problems on Axis IV. DSM improves the reliability of
diagnosis, guides treatment and supports research and communication among
professionals.
35. What are the main activities and services of a clinical psychologist?
The main activities of clinical psychologists are assessment and diagnosis (interviewing,
observation and psychological testing), treatment and psychotherapy for individuals, groups
and families, research into the causes and treatment of psychological problems, teaching
and supervision of trainees, consultation to other professionals and agencies, and prevention
and community work. The largest proportion of clinical psychologists is engaged in private
practice, although they also work in hospitals, clinics, universities and community mental
health centres.
36. Explain the IQ formula and the concept of mental age.
Mental age is the level of intellectual performance typical of an average child of a given
chronological age; for example, a child who performs like an average 8-year-old has a
mental age of 8, whatever his actual age. The intelligence quotient was computed as IQ =
(Mental Age / Chronological Age) x 100. Thus a child whose mental age equals his
chronological age has an IQ of 100 (average), above 100 indicates performance above age
level, and below 100 indicates performance below age level. Later tests, following Wechsler,
replaced this ratio IQ with the deviation IQ based on comparison with one's own age group.
